smt-2020-geometry-01.title: Area from the height
smt-2020-geometry-01.body:
A rhombus circumscribed about a circle of radius $1$ has height $2$ (the distance between opposite sides equals the diameter). If its side is $s$, its area is base times height $=2s$. The height is at most the side, so $s\ge2$, with equality when the rhombus is a square. So the area is at least $4$, attained by the square of side $2$.

**Answer: 4**

smt-2020-geometry-02.title: Tangent lengths
smt-2020-geometry-02.body:
Since $AB\perp BC$ and $BC$ is a diameter, $AB$ is tangent to the circle at $B$. The two tangents from $E$ give $EB=ED$, so $\angle EDB=\angle EBD$. Since $BC$ is a diameter, $\angle BDC=90^\circ$, so $\angle BDA=90^\circ$. Then $\angle EDA=90^\circ-\angle EDB=90^\circ-\angle EBD=\angle EAD$ (in right triangle $ABD$, $\angle EAD=90^\circ-\angle ABD$). So $EA=ED=EB$ and $\frac{AE}{BE}=1$: $E$ is the midpoint of $AB$.

**Answer: 1**

smt-2020-geometry-03.title: Coordinates
smt-2020-geometry-03.body:
Put $A=(0,0)$, $B=(4,0)$, $C=(4,4)$, $D=(0,4)$. Then $P=(4,1)$ and $Q=(1,4)$. Line $AQ$: $y=4x$. Line $DP$: $y=4-\frac34x$. They meet where $4x=4-\frac34x$, so $x=\frac{16}{19}$, $y=\frac{64}{19}$.

By the shoelace formula, $[PQX]=\frac12\left|4\left(4-\frac{64}{19}\right)+1\left(\frac{64}{19}-1\right)+\frac{16}{19}(1-4)\right|=\frac12\cdot\frac{48+45-48}{19}=\frac{45}{38}$.

**Answer: $\frac{45}{38}$**

smt-2020-geometry-03.title: Subtract areas
smt-2020-geometry-03.body:
$[PQX]=[PQD]-[QDX]$. $[PQD]=\frac12\cdot DQ\cdot PC=\frac12\cdot1\cdot3=\frac32$. Triangle $PCD$ is a $3$-$4$-$5$ right triangle, so with $\theta=\angle QDX=\angle CDP$ we have $\sin\theta=\frac35$, $\cos\theta=\frac45$. The area of $QDA$ is $\frac12\cdot1\cdot4=2=[QDX]+[XDA]$, and $[QDX]=\frac12\cdot DQ\cdot DX\sin\theta$, $[XDA]=\frac12\cdot DA\cdot DX\cos(\ldots)$; using the angle $\angle ADX=90^\circ-\theta$ so that $[XDA]=\frac12\cdot4\cdot DX\cos\theta$, we get $2=\frac12DX\left(\sin\theta+4\cos\theta\right)=\frac12DX\cdot\frac{19}5$, so $DX=\frac{20}{19}$. Then $[QDX]=\frac12\cdot1\cdot\frac{20}{19}\cdot\frac35=\frac6{19}$ and $[PQX]=\frac32-\frac6{19}=\frac{45}{38}$.

**Answer: $\frac{45}{38}$**

smt-2020-geometry-04.title: An isosceles trapezoid
smt-2020-geometry-04.body:
$ABCD$ is a kite, so $BD\perp AC$ and $E$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $B$ and $D$. With $AE=12$: $BE=\sqrt{13^2-12^2}=5$ and $DE=\sqrt{15^2-12^2}=9$.

Let $W,X,Y,Z$ be the incenters of $ABE,BCE,CDE,DAE$. The inradius of right triangle $ABE$ (legs $5,12$, hypotenuse $13$) is $\frac{5+12-13}2=2$, the same for $BCE$; for $CDE$ and $DAE$ (legs $9,12$, hypotenuse $15$) it is $\frac{9+12-15}2=3$. The incenters of $ABE$ and $BCE$ are at height $2$ above $AC$ on $B$'s side, symmetric about $BD$, each at distance $2$ from $BD$: $WX=4$. Likewise $YZ=6$ at distance $3$ below $AC$. Both are parallel to $AC$, so $WXYZ$ is an isosceles trapezoid with parallel sides $4$ and $6$ and height $2+3=5$. Its area is $\frac{4+6}2\cdot5=25$.

**Answer: 25**

smt-2020-geometry-05.title: Parity and construction
smt-2020-geometry-05.body:
Every edge lies on exactly two faces, so a face with $2k$ edges contributes $k$ to the total edge count $E=\sum k$. For $E$ to be odd, an odd number of faces must have $k$ odd, i.e. $2\pmod4$ edges. The smallest such face is a hexagon.

*Example with $19$ edges.* Take one hexagonal face and surround it by six quadrilaterals (one on each hexagon edge), adjacent quadrilaterals sharing an edge, then close the six remaining free edges with two more quadrilaterals. This gives a convex polyhedron with $1$ hexagon and $8$ quadrilaterals: $E=\frac{6+8\cdot4}2=19$.

*Minimality (sketch, following the official solution).* A face with $8$ or more sides forces at least $8$ other faces and so at least $16$ further edges, already too many. Three or more hexagons force at least $15$ edges and more than $4$ extra edges are needed to close the polyhedron, again exceeding $19$. With exactly one hexagon and otherwise quadrilaterals the construction above is optimal. So the minimum is $19$.

**Answer: 19**

smt-2020-geometry-06.title: Recognize a 13-14-15 triangle
smt-2020-geometry-06.body:
$AC=\sqrt{\left(\frac{70}{13}\right)^2+\left(\frac{168}{13}\right)^2}=\frac{14}{13}\sqrt{25+144}=14$, so $ABC$ has sides $13,14,15$, area $84$ and semiperimeter $21$; the inradius is $r=\frac{84}{21}=4$.

The angle at $A$ satisfies $\cos A=\frac{13^2+14^2-15^2}{2\cdot13\cdot14}=\frac5{13}$, so $\tan A=\frac{12}5$. The slope of $AC$ is $\frac{168}{70}=\frac{12}5$, so $AB$ is horizontal and $B=(15,3)$. (The other possible $B$, the reflection of this one in line $AC$, is $\left(2-\frac{119}{13},\ 3+\frac{120}{13}\right)$ and has a larger $y$-coordinate.)

The incircle touches $AB$ at distance $s-BC=21-15=6$ from $A$, i.e. at $(8,3)$, and the incenter lies $r=4$ above $AB$ (on the side of $C$): $(8,7)$.

**Answer: $(8,7)$**

smt-2020-geometry-07.title: Ceva's theorem
smt-2020-geometry-07.body:
By the angle bisector theorem $\frac{AF}{FB}=\frac{AC}{BC}=\frac54$, and $\frac{BD}{DC}=1$. Ceva's theorem for the concurrent cevians $AD,BE,CF$ gives $\frac{AF}{FB}\cdot\frac{BD}{DC}\cdot\frac{CE}{EA}=1$, so $\frac{CE}{EA}=\frac45$. With $CE+EA=5$: $CE=\frac{20}9$. In right triangle $BEC$, $BE=\sqrt{16-\frac{400}{81}}=\frac{8\sqrt{14}}9$. The area is $\frac12\cdot AC\cdot BE=\frac12\cdot5\cdot\frac{8\sqrt{14}}9=\frac{20\sqrt{14}}9$.

**Answer: $\frac{20\sqrt{14}}{9}$**

smt-2020-geometry-08.title: Reflections of the circumcircle
smt-2020-geometry-08.body:
Reflecting $H$ in $BC$ gives a point on the circumcircle $\Gamma$ of $ABC$, so the circumcircle of $BHC$ is the reflection of $\Gamma$ in $BC$. Thus $\Gamma_A,\Gamma_B,\Gamma_C$ are the reflections of $\Gamma$ in the three sides, with centers $O_A,O_B,O_C$ (the reflections of the circumcenter $O$), and all of them have radius $R$.

The union consists of the hexagon $AO_CBO_ACO_B$ together with three circular sectors of radius $R$ outside it, centered at $O_A,O_B,O_C$. The hexagon splits into $ABC$ and the triangles $AO_CB\cong AOB$, $BO_AC\cong BOC$, $CO_BA\cong COA$, so its area is $2[ABC]$. The sector at $O_C$ has central angle $360^\circ-\angle AO_CB=360^\circ-2C$, and similarly $360^\circ-2A$ and $360^\circ-2B$ at the other two centers; these add up to $1080^\circ-360^\circ=720^\circ$, so the three sectors have total area $2\pi R^2$.

Numbers: $[ABC]=\sqrt{12\cdot5\cdot4\cdot3}=12\sqrt5$, $R=\frac{7\cdot8\cdot9}{4\cdot12\sqrt5}=\frac{21\sqrt5}{10}$, $R^2=\frac{441}{20}$. The area is $2\pi\cdot\frac{441}{20}+24\sqrt5=\frac{441\pi}{10}+24\sqrt5$.

**Answer: $\frac{441\pi}{10}+24\sqrt5$**

smt-2020-geometry-09.title: Sum of squares to the centroid
smt-2020-geometry-09.body:
For any triangle, $GA^2+GB^2+GC^2=\frac13(AB^2+BC^2+CA^2)$. For a right triangle with hypotenuse $AC$, $AB^2+BC^2=AC^2$, so the sum of the three side squares is $2AC^2$. Thus $\frac23AC^2=156$ and $AC^2=234$.

**Answer: 234**

smt-2020-geometry-10.title: Descartes' circle theorem
smt-2020-geometry-10.body:
The shaded region is the curvilinear triangle between the three mutually tangent circles; the largest circle that fits in it is tangent to all three. With curvatures $k_1=\frac1{23}$, $k_2=\frac1{46}$, $k_3=\frac1{69}$, Descartes' theorem gives for the inner tangent circle
$$k_4=k_1+k_2+k_3+2\sqrt{k_1k_2+k_2k_3+k_3k_1}.$$
Here $k_1+k_2+k_3=\frac1{23}\left(1+\frac12+\frac13\right)=\frac{11}{138}$ and $k_1k_2+k_2k_3+k_3k_1=\frac1{23^2}\left(\frac12+\frac16+\frac13\right)=\frac1{23^2}$, so $k_4=\frac{11}{138}+\frac2{23}=\frac{23}{138}=\frac16$ and the radius is $6$.

**Answer: 6**
